Behaviour #behaviour

That the code's behaviour is checked by something that runs on every change, not taken on trust.

ci-skip-label.1A label skips every CI check
level 1holds gate: ci_runs_testsmeasured · not countedhazard#behaviour
A label skips every CI check on pull requests
Rule
Pull request labels that skip every CI check: is above 0
Why
A label that skips every check lets any pull request merge on a green that no test produced. An agent, or a person in a hurry, needs only to add the label.
Fix
Drop the label condition from the jobs' if: lines, or limit it to jobs that check nothing, such as docs previews. If a skip is needed, scope it with a paths filter so the checks still run on code changes.
Signal
ci_hazards.skip_labels
Scan
ci_hazards · CI that can be told not to fail
ci-test-failures-ignored.1CI ignores test failures
level 1holds gate: ci_runs_testsmeasured · not countedhazard#behaviour
CI ignores test failures
Rule
Committed files that set Maven to ignore test failures: is above 0
Why
With broken tests ignored, the build passes whatever the tests report, so a green run says nothing about the change. A test an agent broke reaches the main branch unseen.
Fix
Remove -Dmaven.test.failure.ignore=true and testFailureIgnore from the CI command, the Jenkinsfile and the poms listed. Quarantine a flaky test by name instead of ignoring every failure.
Signal
ci_hazards.test_failures_ignored
Scan
ci_hazards · CI that can be told not to fail
layer-5-ci.1CI and the agent's local check
level 1gate: ci_runs_testsverified#behaviour
CI runs your tests or linters, and an error stops the job
Rule
A CI check runs on ordinary changes and can stop its job: is true
Why
This turns "the agent says it works" into "CI says it works": a check that can stop its job runs on ordinary changes, so a broken change turns the job red where everyone can see it.
Fix
Add a CI step that runs your test or lint command on pull requests, without || true, continue-on-error or allow_failure.
Signal
ci_checks.enforced_check_runs
Scan
ci_checks · CI runs a test or lint command
layer-6-coverage.1Coverage gates and truth pressure
level 1gate: coverage_gateverified#behaviour
CI runs a coverage gate of at least 50 percent
Rule
CI runs a coverage gate of at least 50 percent: is true
Why
An enforced floor turns the job red when a change takes coverage below it, so tests an agent removes or skips show in CI instead of passing quietly.
Fix
Set a fail_under (or your tool's threshold) of at least 50 percent, written as a number, near your current coverage. Run the coverage check in a CI step on pull requests (pytest --cov, not plain pytest), without || true or continue-on-error. Then CI keeps coverage at the level you have reached.
Signal
coverage_gate.enforced_meets_minimum
Scan
coverage_gate · Coverage gate
layer-6-coverage.2Coverage gates and truth pressure
level 2measuredrequires layer-5-ci.1#behaviour
A mutation run has completed
Rule
A mutation run completed: is true
Why
Coverage shows tests run the code; a mutation run shows whether they notice it changing. A completed run names the surviving mutants, which are the tests an agent cannot yet rely on.
Fix
Run the opt-in mutation pass to see which tests pin behaviour.

skill-script-tests.1Skill script tests
level 1measured#behaviour
Each skill's scripts have tests beside them (presence, not coverage)
Rule
Skills whose scripts have no tests beside them: is 0
Why
A skill's scripts run with an agent's permissions every time it triggers; tests beside them are the only check that a change still does what the SKILL.md promises.
Fix
Add tests for each named skill's scripts in that skill's own folder (tests/ or test_*.py beside them); where the report finds them elsewhere, move or copy them in, since tests outside the folder do not ship with the skill.

Contracts #contracts

That generated output and its source agree, so an agent editing one does not quietly break the other.

api-compat.1API compatibility checked by CI
level 1measured#contracts#structure
API compatibility checked by CI
Rule
CI runs an API compatibility check: is true
Why
An agent changing code cannot see who depends on its public names. A compatibility tool CI runs against the last release, or a test that pins the exports, turns the job red on a change that breaks a caller, so the contract holds without a reviewer catching it.
Fix
Run a compatibility check in CI: cargo semver-checks, buf breaking or api-extractor run. apidiff only prints a report, so exit 1 when its output lists a change. japicmp needs --error-on-* or a breakBuild* setting. Or run a test that compares the exports with a fixed list.
Signal
api_compat.present
Scan

Clear modules let an agent load the part of the code a task touches, instead of tracing the whole repository to change one thing.

An agent job can rewrite its own instructions
Rule
Agent jobs that can rewrite unowned instruction or workflow files: is above 0

An agent job that can push files can change AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or its own workflow, so the next run follows instructions no reviewer approved. CI then checks changes against rules the agent wrote for itself.

Agent runtime #agent_runtime

That an agent can see the system it changes run, and confirm a change there, not only in the code.

agent-evals.1Agent eval suites run in CI with a baseline
level 1measured#agent_runtime#behaviour
Agent eval suites run in CI with a baseline
Rule
An agent eval suite runs in CI against a committed baseline: is true
Why
A prompt or model change can make an agent worse while every unit test still passes. Eval cases run in CI against a committed baseline turn that drop into a red check, and the baseline in the tree says what passing means.
Fix
Keep the agent's eval cases in an evals/ folder and commit a baseline beside them: a snapshot, recorded model responses or a tool-budget file. Run the folder from a CI job, gated to prompt and model changes if it costs money.

An agent job with a write scope and no separate writer job can push, merge or edit issues on the strength of text an outsider wrote, with nothing between the prompt and the write.
Fix
Drop the write scopes from the agent job's `permissions:` and do the writes in a job that `needs:` it, or in gh-aw `safe-outputs:`. A turn or budget cap limits cost, not what the token can do.

agent-least-privilege.1Agent jobs run with least privilege
level 1measured#agent_runtime#governance
Agent jobs run with least privilege
Rule
Every agent job runs with a read-only token: is true
Why
An agent acts on whatever text reaches its prompt, an issue body or a pull request included. A read-only token keeps a misled agent from pushing, merging or editing issues itself; a separate job that acts on its output does the writing, where a reviewer can see each write.
Fix
Give each job that runs an agent `permissions:` with no write scope, such as `contents: read` or `read-all`. Move writes into a separate job that `needs:` the agent job, or into gh-aw `safe-outputs:`. A job-level `permissions:` replaces the workflow's, so check the agent job's own block.

model-ci-gated.1Model-backed CI jobs are gated
level 1measured#governance
Model-backed CI jobs are gated
Rule
Model-backed CI jobs that run on every change without a gate: is 0
Why
A CI job that calls a model costs money on every run. If it runs on every merge and every pull request update, the cost grows with the number of changes agents make, not with changes to the prompts it tests.
Fix
Run each named job only when prompts, skills or instruction files change, or nightly, or on a label. Cancel superseded runs, sample the eval cases, and use the cheapest model that still tells good from bad. Move rule-checkable assertions into ordinary tests.

Configure the checks

Each option below changes what a run checks or how CI acts on it. Settings in .assess/config.toml are committed, so every run and every teammate reads the same ones.

Leave out a check for your repository

Add a [checks] table to .assess/config.toml and list each condition id to leave out. The ids are the ones on the cards above.

Each entry needs a reason. An entry without one is skipped with a warning, and the check stays in force.

kind is one of not_applicable, measured_elsewhere, tool_unsupported, false_positive or other, the default.

An excluded condition earns nothing and costs nothing. A Step gate it covers stays unmet while the exclusion stands.

.assess/config.toml
[checks]
exclude = [
  { id = "layer-6-coverage.1", kind = "measured_elsewhere",
    reason = "Coverage is enforced in the release pipeline repository." },
]

Reference: Owner exclusions in the scoring model · #910

Choose a profile

A run scores against the default maturity model unless you name another.

--profile handover is the bar a production team expects before it owns a repository. --profile citizen is a lighter bar while a citizen developer builds.

A profile run leaves the committed .assess/prior-level.json baseline as the default model's. The CI gate keeps comparing default runs.

Claude Code
/assess --profile handover

Reference: Named profiles, #1150

Write your own model

--levels FILE scores against a maturity model you write, in the format of levels/default.toml.

/fleet --levels FILE reads the same file, so one repository gets the same Step from both.

Claude Code
/assess --levels .assess/our-model.toml

Reference: The default model · Build your own practice

Count central guardrails

Claude Code managed settings live on the machine, not in the repository, so a run leaves them out by default.

Pass --managed-settings, or set managed_settings = true under [agent_ops], to count them toward the agent permissions practice.

A central deny rule then counts, graded as listed. The config key is read by single-repository runs only; /fleet takes the flag.

Claude Code
/assess --managed-settings
.assess/config.toml
[agent_ops]
managed_settings = true

Reference: The /assess skill · #1153

Turn on the regression gate in CI

fail_on_gate_loss turns a pull request red when a Step gate your committed baseline held now reads unmet. An example is CI no longer running the tests.

The baseline is .assess/prior-level.json, which every /assess run writes. Commit your .assess/ directory first; until then the job passes and says so.

Set fail_on_gate_loss = true under [gate] in .assess/config.toml for every CI host. On the command line, assess_gate.py --fail-on-gate-loss is the same switch.

The GitHub Action is warn-only by default; its fail_on_gate_loss input turns the gate on.

The GitLab CI template turns the gate on by default. Its fail_on_gate_loss: false input keeps the job green on a lost gate.

An input or the flag can only turn the gate on. With fail_on_gate_loss = true in the config, false in an input changes nothing.

.assess/config.toml
[gate]
fail_on_gate_loss = true
.github/workflows/assess-gate.yml (steps)
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1  # v7.0.1
    with:
      fetch-depth: 0   # full history for churn and the baseline
  - uses: bjcoombs/ai-native-toolkit@v4.1.0
    with:
      config: .assess/config.toml
      fail_on_gate_loss: 'true'
.gitlab-ci.yml
include:
  - remote: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bjcoombs/ai-native-toolkit/v4.1.0/templates/assess-gate.yml
    inputs:
      config: .assess/config.toml
      fail_on_gate_loss: true

Reference: Use as a GitHub Action · Use in GitLab CI · action.yml inputs · GitLab template inputs
